title: Pain Assessment

unit.title: Clinical Office Practice and Patient Safety

sections.learningObjectives:
- Select and administer an appropriate pain assessment scale for a patient's age and abilities.
- Document the patient's own report of pain accurately, in their own words and without personal interpretation.
- Record the pain score together with the scale used, along with relevant details such as location, quality, and onset.
- Recognize the scope of the medical office assistant and avoid diagnosing or judging the cause of pain.
- Report pain and any concerning changes promptly to the clinician.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Think of the scale like a thermometer for pain: 0 means it is totally off and there is no pain, and 10 means it is turned up all the way to the worst pain you can imagine.

### Question 2

A higher number is just the patient telling you the pain feels bigger or stronger, like turning up the volume dial. It is not a guess about how sick they are.

### Question 3

Instead of asking a child to pick a number, you show them a row of faces, from a big smile to a crying face, and they point to the face that shows how they feel inside.

### Question 4

When a baby or a person cannot talk, you watch how they act, like whether they cry or move their legs, and use those clues to score how much pain they seem to be in.

### Question 5

Imagine a straight line like a road: one end is no pain and the other end is the worst pain ever. The patient puts a mark on the road to show where their pain sits.

### Question 6

Instead of numbers or faces, you give the person word choices like a little, medium, or a lot, and they pick the word that fits.

### Question 7

Pain is like a feeling that only the person can know for sure, the way only you know how much a pinch hurts. So we ask the person and believe what they tell us.

### Question 8

You would not hand a word puzzle to someone who cannot read. In the same way, you pick the pain scale that the patient can actually understand and use.

### Question 9

Just like the office checks your temperature and heartbeat every visit to see how you are doing, it also asks about pain, because pain is an important clue about how a person feels.

### Question 10

When someone cannot tell you they hurt, you look for clues: a scrunched-up face, holding an arm or belly, or a moaning sound can mean they are in pain.

### Question 11

It is a row of six faces, like a set of emojis, going from a big smile to a crying face, and the person points to the face that shows how they feel.

### Question 12

You show the person the rules of the game before they play, so they know what 0 and 10 mean and can give a number that really fits.

### Question 13

If you measure your height with a different ruler every day, the numbers will not match up. Using the same ruler, or scale, lets you see if pain is going up or down over time.

### Question 14

If you ask a friend how their day was using different words each time, it is hard to compare answers. Asking the same way makes the answers easier to compare.

### Question 15

You can repeat the rules, but you must not hand the person an answer, because then it is your guess, not theirs.

### Question 16

You write down exactly what the person told you, like taking dictation, and you also write which measuring tool you used.

### Question 17

You write down what the person said and also what you saw, like a reporter who writes both the quote and the facts without choosing sides.

### Question 18

You show the child the faces and explain that the smile means no hurt and the crying face means the most hurt, then let the child point.

### Question 19

You ask the child what they feel, like asking them to point at the face, and you also listen to the grown-up who knows them, because both clues help.

### Question 20

When someone cannot tell you they hurt, you become a careful watcher, looking for signs like a tight face or a held arm, and you share what you saw.

### Question 21

If your friend said their cookie was a 7 out of 10 and you wrote down a 4 just to match yesterday, you would be writing a lie about their cookie. Same idea with pain.

### Question 22

If two people do not share a language, you bring in someone trained to translate, so the patient can tell you in their own words how much it hurts.

### Question 23

You write down exactly what the person said, using their words like a quote in a book, so nothing they meant gets changed.

### Question 24

To tell someone about a pain, you say where it is, what it feels like, how strong it is, and when it started, like the important details of a story.

### Question 25

The P is about what makes the pain worse and what makes it better, like asking whether standing up or lying down helps.

### Question 26

Onset is the start of the pain story, like asking when the trouble first began and what the person was doing.

### Question 27

Quality is the flavor of the pain, like describing a food as spicy or sweet, but for pain it is words like sharp, dull, or heavy.

### Question 28

Radiation is where the pain wanders to, like a puddle that spreads from one spot to a bigger area.

### Question 29

If a problem is getting better, you write that down too, so the doctor knows the medicine or treatment is working.

### Question 30

You write down the facts and the person's own words, the way a good news reporter writes only what they saw and heard, with no opinions added.

### Question 31

You write things down right away, the way you jot down a phone message as soon as you hear it, so you do not forget the details.

### Question 32

It is like telling someone both what you measured and what the person told you, so they get the full story rather than only half of it.

### Question 33

You write down what the person said, plain and simple, without adding whether you think it is a big deal or not.

### Question 34

These are the 'what makes it worse' and 'what makes it better' details, like noting that a bump hurts more when you press it and feels better when you rest.

### Question 35

Pain is invisible to everyone but the patient, so you trust what they tell you, write it down, and pass it along, even if they look fine.

### Question 36

You write down the exact spot, like 'left shoulder,' the way you would give precise directions instead of saying 'over there.'

### Question 37

Even when the answer is 'no pain,' you write down the zero, because it tells the doctor that today the pain meter reads nothing at all.

### Question 38

You are the helper who writes down the clues and hands them to the detective; you do not solve the mystery yourself.

### Question 39

Your job is to write down what the person says and pass it to the doctor, not to decide whether they are telling the truth.

### Question 40

You are the note-taker and messenger, making sure the doctor gets the information, not the one who decides what is wrong or what medicine to give.

### Question 41

If someone has a very high pain score and also has trouble breathing, you tell the doctor right away, like pulling a fire alarm instead of waiting.

### Question 42

Writing 'the patient is being dramatic' is adding your own unkind opinion, like writing 'this person complains too much' in a school report.

### Question 43

Documenting is taking a photo of the facts; interpreting is writing a caption saying what you think the facts mean. Your job is the photo.

### Question 44

If someone hurts in two different places, you write down both places, like listing every place you got a scrape instead of just one.

### Question 45

You are asked to check the meter again and tell the doctor the new number, not to decide for yourself whether the medicine worked.

### Question 46

If a pain that is usually the same suddenly gets a lot worse or different, that is a new clue that the doctor needs to hear about right away.

### Question 47

You tell the doctor both what the person said and what you saw, like reporting a smell of smoke and a beeping alarm together.

### Question 48

You hand the important note to the person in charge of the patient's care, like giving a message to the right teacher, not just anyone.

### Question 49

When the number jumps way up from last time, you flag it for the doctor, like noticing the temperature on a weather map suddenly got much hotter.

### Question 50

Chest pain is like a smoke alarm; you treat it as an emergency and get help right away, even if it might turn out to be nothing.

### Question 51

You write it in the official record and also tell the doctor, the way you both write down a message and give it to the person.

### Question 52

If someone does not want to pick a number, you write down that they chose not to, instead of making up a number for them.

### Question 53

You put each piece of information in its labeled box, the way you sort mail into the right slots, so it can be found later.

### Question 54

Keeping important health information a secret from the doctor would be like hiding a broken step from a repair person; it only makes things less safe.

### Question 55

Knowing the pain stops someone from sleeping or doing normal things tells the doctor how much it is really bothering them, like explaining how a problem affects your whole day.

### Question 56

Documenting writes down the facts and the patient's words; interpreting is guessing the reason, which is the doctor's job, not yours.

### Question 57

Chronic pain is the kind that sticks around for a long time, like a song that stays on repeat for months, while acute pain is new and brief.

### Question 58

Acute pain is the fresh kind, like a new cut or a sudden headache, that just started a short while ago.

### Question 59

You make sure the person can see your face and the scale, the way you would write a note down for someone who cannot hear well.

### Question 60

When asked what the person said, you repeat their exact words, like retelling a message word for word instead of making up your own version.

### Question 61

You write down both what the person said and what you saw, like reporting both a witness's words and what the camera recorded.

### Question 62

You do your job, which is writing down and passing along the information, and you leave the big decisions to the doctor.

### Question 63

You write down today's real number, and you leave yesterday's number alone, even if they are different, because both are true for their own days.

### Question 64

You write down what the person already took, like noting the ingredients someone used, and share it with the doctor so they know the full picture.

### Question 65

Asking everyone about pain the same kind way is like making sure every student gets a turn to speak, so no one is skipped.

### Question 66

The patient's own words about how they feel go in the 'what the patient said' box, while things you can measure go in the 'what we observed' box.

### Question 67

Objective means what you can see with your own eyes, like watching someone hold their belly, instead of what they tell you they feel.

### Question 68

You write down what they said and gently ask them to also pick a number, so you have both their words and a score to compare.

### Question 69

Writing the number down is step one, but you also have to tell the doctor, like putting up a note and also speaking to the teacher.

### Question 70

You write down that it is both knees, not just one, the way you would note that both hands, not one, are muddy.

### Question 71

The assistant gathers the puzzle pieces and hands them over, and the doctor puts the puzzle together and decides what to do.

### Question 72

The pain scale is like a 'how do you feel?' question that only the person feeling the pain can answer for themselves.

### Question 73

The four usual checks are temperature, pulse, breathing, and blood pressure, and pain is added as a fifth check because it is an important clue too.

### Question 74

If talking is hard, you let the person point to a picture that shows how they feel, the way you might point to a menu item you want.

### Question 75

Pain is like how spicy a food tastes; two people can feel the same thing very differently, so only the person's own answer counts.

### Question 76

If someone gives two different answers, you kindly ask again to make sure you understand, and write down their final answer.

### Question 77

Timing is about when the pain shows up, like whether it is there all day or only sometimes, the way you describe a clock schedule.

### Question 78

A leading question is like whispering an answer to someone before they respond; you should let them answer for themselves.

### Question 79

You write down both things you noticed, the pain and the high blood pressure, and hand both to the doctor, without guessing how they are connected.

### Question 80

Washing hands before and after helping someone is like cleaning a shared spoon between uses, so germs do not spread.

### Question 81

FLACC is an easy word that spells out five things to watch: Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, and Consolability, which means how easy the person is to comfort.

### Question 82

Counting from 0 to 10 gives 11 numbers, like counting your fingers starting from zero plus ten more.

### Question 83

Writing down which ruler you used means the number still makes sense later, like labeling a photo with where it was taken.

### Question 84

If someone is not sure between two numbers, you write down that they said both, or ask them to pick one, instead of choosing for them.

### Question 85

If a new pain shows up somewhere different and is a lot stronger, that is a new clue the doctor needs to hear about right away, like a new warning light turning on.
